newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU parliament seeks interim government in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament seeks interim government in Zaire.

text.p: The European Parliament on Thursday urged Zaire's President Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila urgently to form an interim government to organise democratic elections and avert a bloody conflict.

The call came as South African President Nelson Mandela, unbowed by the postponement on Wednesday of Zairean peace talks in Congo, invited Kabila to Cape Town to discuss a South African initiative aimed at preventing a violent civil war showdown.

The European Union's directly elected assembly called on EU governments to give substantial support to United Nations special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who has been working closely with the South Africans to broker a peaceful transition to democracy in Zaire after more than 30 years of autocratic rule by Mobutu.
A spokesman for President Mandela said on Thursday that with the exception of France, which had raised some concerns, most African and Western governments supported the South African peace plan.
This calls for a legal transitional structure to replace Zaire's present constitutional government and internationally supervised democratic elections.
Mobutu agreed at face-to-face talks with Kabila on May 4 to hand power to an elected president, but no arrangements were agreed.
Kabila, both then and in public statements since, has insisted Mobutu hand power at once to his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
Euro-deputies, who have voiced concern about the rebel leader's commitment to democracy, demanded a UN investigation into massacres of Rwandan Hutu rebels in rebel-held areas.
The UN's Sahnoun said on Wednesday he and Mandela had not lost hope of a peace deal. "We are not going to give up. We will continue to try to avoid another humanitarian tragedy," he said.
Mobutu, 66, who is reputed to have amassed a huge personal fortune over the years, seized power in 1965. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against communism.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, have made lightning advances across the impoverished, corruption-plagued nation.
Rebel radio suggested Kabila's forces were nearing the approaches to Kinshasa. The government dismissed such reports.
